name: Intracavernosal alprostadil
question: How did intracavernosal alprostadil perform against placebo in erectile response and during home self-injection for erectile dysfunction?

design.blinding: Double-blind placebo-controlled dose-response study; single-blind dose-finding study; open-label home-use study
design.population: Men with vasculogenic, neurogenic, psychogenic, or mixed erectile dysfunction contributed 296 dose-response, 201 dose-finding, and 683 home self-injection study enrolments; 12 dose-finding and 40 home-use participants had also joined the dose-response study.
design.description: Three prospective studies, including randomized placebo comparison
design.locator: Full text, Methods, pp 873–874; Results, pp 874–875; n is summed study enrolments, not unique patients

verdictNote: Every tested dose exceeded placebo; the home-use study was open-label.
takeaway: In a randomized, double-blind study of 296 men, intracavernosal alprostadil 2.5–20 µg produced more clinical and RigiScan erectile responses than placebo (0/59 responders). In a separate, open-label six-month study of 683 men, sexual activity was reported possible after 94% of injections.

reports.label: Dose response, dose finding, and six-month home use
reports.citation: Linet OI, Ogrinc FG. "Efficacy and Safety of Intracavernosal Alprostadil in Men with Erectile Dysfunction." *N Engl J Med.* 1996;334(14):873-877. doi:10.1056/NEJM199604043341401
reports.followUp: Single-injection dose response; six-month self-injection cohort
reports.followUpLocator: Full text, Methods, pp 874–875; Results, pp 875–876

results.measure: Full clinical rigidity or RigiScan rigidity ≥70% for ≥10 minutes after one fixed-dose injection (2.5, 5, 10, or 20 µg) versus placebo; intention-to-treat analysis of men receiving ≥1 injection

values.exp: 2.5 µg: n=57; 5 µg: n=60; 10 µg: n=62; 20 µg: n=58; each dose superior to placebo for both assessments (P<0.01 or P<0.001); clinical dose response P<0.001

results.note: Pairwise P values apply to each dose versus placebo; the trend P applies to increasing doses. The paper does not state a prespecified alpha or numeric response rates by dose; Figure 1 is graphical.
results.locator: Full text, Methods, Dose–Response Study and Statistical Analysis, p 874; Results and Figure 1, pp 874–875

results.measure: Minimal effective dose ≤2 µg (RigiScan rigidity ≥70% for ≥10 minutes) by erectile dysfunction cause among 135 dose-finding completers
results.note: Single-blind dose-finding study enrolled 201 men; these subgroup fractions are for the 135 completers. Initial dose 0.5 µg, escalated to 30 µg as needed.
results.locator: Full text, Methods, Dose-Finding Study, p 874; Results, Dose-Finding Study, p 875

results.measure: Proportion of injections followed by reported ability to have sexual activity over six months

values.exp: 94% of injections; injection-level denominator not stated for this measure

results.note: 683 enrolled; 577 began home self-injection. The 94% ability measure is stated in the abstract without its injection denominator.
results.locator: Full text, Abstract, p 873; Methods, Study of Efficacy and Safety, p 874; Results, p 875

results.measure: Proportion of injections after which sexual activity was rated satisfactory

values.exp: men 11,924/13,762 (87%) rated injections with recorded sexual activity satisfactory, including 11,223 intercourse and 701 masturbation; partners 8,496/9,892 (86%); 507/551 men (92%) reported satisfactory sexual activity at least once

results.note: Satisfaction denominators include injections with ratings; 551 men reported sexual-activity information and 552 partners contributed ratings.
results.locator: Full text, Results, Study of Efficacy and Safety, p 875; Table 1, p 876

harms.label: Penile pain

values.exp: 343/683 men (50%) at some time; 1,873/16,575 injections (11%); 43/683 men (6%) withdrew because of pain

harms.locator: Full text, Results, Study of Efficacy and Safety, p 875; Table 2, p 877

harms.label: Prolonged erection and priapism

values.exp: 35/683 men (5%) prolonged erection (4–6 hours), including 3 discontinuations; 5/683 (1%) priapism (>6 hours), one requiring drug therapy

harms.locator: Full text, Methods, p 874; Results, p 876; Table 2, p 877

harms.label: Fibrotic complication and injection-site bleeding

values.exp: 15/683 men (2%) penile fibrotic complications, including 9 Peyronie’s disease, 4 curvature/deviation, 2 nodules; 57/683 (8%) hematoma or ecchymosis

harms.locator: Full text, Results, p 876; Table 2, p 877

harms.label: Systemic medical events

values.exp: 39/683 men (6%) had possibly related systemic medical events, none serious; 9/683 (1%) had symptoms potentially related to hypotension

harms.locator: Full text, Results, Study of Efficacy and Safety, p 876

delivery.label: Drug and study structure
delivery.value: Double-blind, single 1-mL injection of placebo (n=59) or alprostadil 2.5 µg (n=57), 5 µg (n=60), 10 µg (n=62), or 20 µg (n=58); separate single-blind dose-finding study started at 0.5 µg and escalated to 30 µg; open-label home-use study followed 683 men for six months.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods, Dose–Response Study, Dose-Finding Study, and Study of Efficacy and Safety, p 874

delivery.label: Office titration and home-treatment uptake
delivery.value: An adequate office-titrated dose (erection sufficient for penetration, lasting ≤60 minutes) was established for 606/683 men (89%); 577/606 began home self-injection, 471/683 (69%) completed six months. Of 577 home users, 247 (43%) kept the initial dose, 231 (40%) increased it, and 99 (17%) reduced it; mean dose was 17.7 µg initially and 20.7 µg at six months.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods, Study of Efficacy and Safety, p 874; Results, p 875

delivery.label: Injection technique
delivery.value: A 27–30-gauge half-inch needle was inserted perpendicular to the taut penis at either side of the base, avoiding visible veins; pressure was applied for five minutes or until bleeding stopped. Men were trained before home use, kept injection and intercourse diaries, and attended monthly visits.

reports.label: Quality of life through 18 months
reports.dateLocator: PubMed PMID 9146597 and Crossref: June 1997; publication day not specified
reports.citation: Willke RJ, Glick HA, McCarron TJ, et al. "Quality of Life Effects of Alprostadil Therapy for Erectile Dysfunction." *J Urol.* 1997;157(6):2124-2128. doi:10.1016/S0022-5347(01)64692-5
reports.followUp: CMSH-SFQ and Duke Health Profile at 3, 6, 12, and 18 months; Brief Symptom Inventory at 6, 12, and 18 months
reports.followUpLocator: Full text, Methods, Quality of life outcomes, p 2125

results.measure: Weighted paired change from baseline to 6 months (or next nearest visit) in four CMSH-SFQ domains, scored 0–100 (higher is better)

values.exp: Frequency: baseline 17.7, change +2.3 (P=0.0004); erection: 44.3, +33.9 (P=0.0001); orgasm: 63.4, +12.3 (P=0.0001); satisfaction: 47.5, +25.3 (P=0.0001); paired n=397–513 across domains

results.note: Ten questionnaire items improved at all post-initiation visits; joint test of four domain changes P<0.001. Inverse-probability weighting addressed nonresponse; no concurrent control or multiplicity adjustment.
results.locator: Full text, Methods, Quality of life outcomes and Analysis, p 2125; Table 2 and Results, p 2126

results.measure: Weighted paired change from baseline to 6 months (or next nearest visit) in Brief Symptom Inventory scores, scaled 0–4 (lower is better)

values.exp: Interpersonal sensitivity: baseline 0.248, change −0.053 (P=0.0005); anxiety: 0.234, −0.046 (P=0.0007); depression: 0.245, −0.052 (P=0.0004); global severity: 0.246, −0.034 (P=0.0002); paired n=449–457 across domains

results.note: P=0.006 is the joint test of nine multiple-question domains; inverse-probability weighted, uncontrolled paired analysis.
results.locator: Full text, Methods, Quality of life outcomes and Analysis, p 2125; Table 2 and Results, p 2126

results.measure: Weighted paired change from baseline to 6 months (or next nearest visit) in Duke Health Profile scores (0–100; direction varies by domain)

values.exp: Mental health: baseline 79.8, change +2.09 (P=0.002); self-esteem: 79.3, +2.00 (P=0.001); pain: 29.2, +3.48 (worse; P=0.018); perceived health: 85.3, −2.42 (P=0.053); paired n=484–495 across domains

results.note: P<0.001 is the joint test of five disjoint domains. Pain worsened despite improvement in mental health; no multiplicity adjustment.
results.locator: Full text, Methods, Quality of life outcomes and Analysis, p 2125; Table 2 and Results, p 2126

results.measure: Changes from baseline at 3, 6, 12 and 18 months among respondents with paired scores at each visit

values.exp: Most sexual-function and Duke Health Profile changes persisted through 18 months; erection score fell 2.5 points from month 12 to 18 (P=0.02)

results.note: Longitudinal results are available-case, unweighted comparisons; the statistically significant 12-to-18-month decline concerns the erection domain.
results.locator: Full text, Methods, Quality of life outcomes and Analysis, p 2125; Figure and Results, Duration of effect, pp 2126–2127

harms.label: Pain cited in treatment discontinuation

values.exp: Among 115 dropout-questionnaire respondents, pain during erection was a major reason for 19.3%; injection pain was a major reason for 17.3%

harms.locator: Full text, Table 3 and Results, Reasons for discontinuing therapy, p 2127
harms.note: Reasons among questionnaire respondents, not incidence of treatment-emergent adverse events.

delivery.label: Home self-injection and completion
delivery.value: Of 683 enrolled men at 33 US sites, 579 entered open-label, flexible-dose self-injection after office dose titration, with recommended use 1–3 times weekly; 471 completed the initial 6 months, 416 entered the 1-year extension, and 321 completed it.
delivery.locator: Full text, Methods, Clinical trial, pp 2124–2125

delivery.label: Discontinuation questionnaire
delivery.value: Across the initial and extension phases, 203 men discontinued and 115 returned questionnaires. Failure to achieve a firm erection contributed at least as a minor factor for 52.3% of respondents and was the major reason for 26.6%.
delivery.locator: Full text, Results, Reasons for discontinuing therapy and Table 3, pp 2126–2127
